newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritians seek actions to spur economy.
newsitem.headline: Mauritians seek actions to spur economy.

text.p: Mauritian entrepreneurs are urging the government to improve infrastructure on the Indian Ocean island and to encourage new investment to counter the current wait-and-see attitude of business, financial analysts said.
They see that as the only way Finance Minister Vasant Bunwaree can meet the ambitious economic targets he set last month and which have prompted a major recovery on the stock exchange.
Bunwaree was made finance minister in October and his task remains to convince markets that Mauritius, the island known as "paradise", is set for growth.

"1997 is the year to translate (political) intentions into action, if we want to transform Mauritius into a small economic power house," entrepreneur and Export Processing Zone (EPZ) Development Authority chairman George Chung told Reuters.

"The government will have to lead and not just follow the bandwagon. It needs government to spend investment money; not to increase (civil service) wages with no productivity gains, to shape up the country's future," Chung said.

The coalition government of Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam swept to power in a landslide victory in December 1995 on the back of pledges that it would maintain economic growth and improve living standards.
Economic analysts say the pledges have yet to be fulfilled.
Bunwaree wants to restore confidence in economic policy and has set a target of increasing gross domestic product by 5.5 to 6.5 percent a year in the next three years.
GDP growth was 5.7 percent in 1996 and 5.3 percent in 1995. The government has not forecast growth in 1997.

Bunwaree wants to boost investment to 30 percent of GDP by the year 2000 from a stagnant 24.5 percent, and to raise the private sector's share of investment to 80 percent from 65 percent in the same period.
Gross domestic product at factor cost in 1996 was estimated at 67.17 billion rupees ($3.38 billion) in this island of 1.1 million inhabitants.
Financial analysts urged the government to liberalise air access, maritime transport and telecommunications and to step up investments in the airport and improve roads and water supply.
They wanted more manpower training to improve productivity in the wake of increasingly liberalised trade and global competition.
Azad Jeetun, director of the influential private sector body Mauritius Employers' Federation (MEF), told Reuters: "If nothing is done, the situation will worsen."
Economists said growth in 1996 resulted from gains in tourism and from textiles, which should continue to drive the economy in 1997 and 1998.
In 1996, tourist arrivals rose by 13.6 percent to 480,000 from 422,463 in 1995 and are expected to exceed 500,000 in 1997.
The value of shipments from the export-processing zone grew by 12.2 percent to 20.5 billion rupees in 1996 from 18.3 billion rupees in 1995. They are forecast to rise to 22.5 billion rupees in 1997.
Chung said that for the longer term, Mauritius should aim at regional cooperation for sustainable economic growth.

"The first economic boom came with sugar, the second with textiles and if there is a third one, it will come from the region with Mauritius as a hub centre for trade, textiles-led manufacturing and industry," he said, referring to the island's strategy of developing its freeport into an economic pillar.
"Access within the region should definitely be made much easier," Chung told Reuters.
($1=20 Mauritian rupees).
